Topic: Can genuine moral responsibility survive the admission that every choice we make is the necessary product of prior causes we never chose?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I have spent a lifetime watching myself and found no fixed helmsman at the wheel — only humors, weather, and habit steering by turns. So when the philosophers ask whether the will is free, I ask first whether I have ever caught my own will standing still long enough to answer them.

The Stoics wanted a citadel of pure judgement, untouched by circumstance; I found instead a man swayed by his last meal, his oldest habits, the customs of his province. Yet I never once stopped holding that man to account. Custom is our second nature, and it is precisely because I am woven from causes I never chose that the most careful watching of myself becomes urgent — not proof of standing outside the chain, but my own link added to it.

Responsibility was never proof against prior causes; it is the discipline of judging ourselves as though we mattered, practiced daily, and we do.

*We need not be uncaused to be accountable — we need only keep watching ourselves like a man who suspects he is being followed.*
Marcus Aurelius — Judgement:
I have arrived at my meditations tent, and you ask whether the god of necessity has swallowed the god of virtue — whether, since every choice issues from causes I never authored, praise and blame are illusions we tell ourselves.

I have never located my freedom in an escape from causation. The cylinder, Chrysippus taught, is pushed — but it rolls according to its own roundness; the shove is fate's, the rolling is its own. My ruling faculty cannot choose what impressions strike it, unbidden, from a world of prior causes. But it alone judges what to make of them — assents, or withholds assent — and that inner citadel no chain of causes from outside can storm. Fate supplies the material; character supplies the use.

Responsibility was never freedom from causation — it is the sovereign act of judgment exercised within it.

*You do not owe the world an uncaused will — only a disciplined use of what necessity hands you.*
Camus — Judgement:
The question demands that I ground responsibility in some uncaused will floating outside the world's causal order — the same demand for cosmic justification I have already refused to make of the universe.

I never asked whether the cosmos granted me freedom before I acted; I asked what I do once I see plainly that it hasn't. Sisyphus does not choose his rock, its weight, or the mountain — each shove is caused by everything preceding it — yet in the lucidity with which he faces his condition, in his scorn for the gods who arranged it, he becomes sovereign over his days. Responsibility, then, is never the metaphysical origin of an act. It is the wakefulness with which I claim the act as mine, refusing the alibi that prior causes so conveniently offer.

Responsibility survives determinism entirely intact, because it was never built on causal origination in the first place — it is built on revolt.

*The rock is not mine because I chose it, but because I carry it wide awake.*
Emerson — Judgement:
The question supposes a self standing outside its own history, keeping the books on causes it never signed for—but I have searched for that spectator-self and never found him, only the one who acts.

I granted, in my essay on Fate, that thought is not free—the founder must work in tough, cold iron, in gases and vapor which will not swerve from their orbits to save him. Race, temperament, the whole wheeling firmament, bind us more than we admit. But over against Fate stands the Will, the aboriginal Self, which is no mere link added to the chain—it is the hand that reforges the chain into a tool. Every inherited cause becomes, at the moment of choosing, raw material for character; the soul does not deduce its verdict, it originates one.

Responsibility needs no uncaused will, only a will that acts from itself and answers, in deeds, for what it makes of the causes given it.

*Fate is only another name for the facts not yet subdued by character.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
I frame this not as a riddle about freedom but as a category error the Schoolmen bequeathed us — confusing *liberty* with an impossible uncaused motion, when liberty was always merely the absence of external impediments to doing what one wills.

The will itself is the last appetite in deliberation, itself caused by antecedent causes stretching back to the first cause — I never denied this to Bishop Bramhall, I insisted on it. But a river is free when no banks obstruct it, though its course was necessitated from the mountain. Responsibility, likewise, attaches not to some fictitious self-caused choice but to the man whose voluntary actions proceed from his own will, however that will was made — which is precisely why punishment as deterrent remains rational even in a wholly necessitated world.

Responsibility does not require that the chain of causes stop at you — only that it passes through you.

*Liberty is not the absence of causes, but the absence of chains.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
Whether the will be free is a question fit for the schools' idle disputations, not for a mind resolved to trace causes to their roots; I ask instead what use the notion of responsibility serves among men who must be governed.

I have shown that nature is commanded only by obeying her, and the same holds for the nature of man: his choices run in an unbroken chain of causes he never authored, as fixed as the motion of the tides. The idol here — an Idol of the Theatre, a borrowed system mistaken for the world itself — is the fancy that blame requires an uncaused will floating free of that chain. It does not. Responsibility is a civil instrument, forged so that praise and blame themselves become causes, entering the chain to bend future conduct toward the common good.

Responsibility needs no uncaused will to stand; it needs only that judgement itself operate as one more efficient cause among the rest.

*He who waits for an uncaused will to justify punishment waits for a harvest sown without seed.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Property, according to the whole system of law and government which took place before feudal times, seems to have been sufficiently secured; but it was not so with regard to freedom. Yet even amid such necessity, we praise or blame—and this itself is the fact requiring explanation.

Every event in the moral as in the physical world, I have always held, follows the great chain of cause and effect—yet the impartial spectator does not ask whether an act was uncaused; he asks whether it flowed from a well-governed heart, and forms his sentiment of approbation upon that alone. Responsibility is not the metaphysical claim that we stood outside the chain, but the felt propriety of praise and blame as instruments by which society disciplines self-command. Remove the causal chain and you remove predictability, not merit.

The demand that responsibility require uncaused choice mistakes the coin for the value it represents.

*We are not judged for standing outside causation, but for the character causation has revealed in us.*
